summary:
The literature says Israeli voting is organised around group identity, and most movement happens inside the two blocs rather than between them. Since Shamir and Arian (1999), and in INES analyses through 2022, the vote has been structured by "identity" issues: territory and security, religion and state, Jewish-Arab relations and, more recently, the Supreme Court. Economics barely separates the blocs. Affective polarisation between the two big camps peaked at 6.2 in 2022 (it was 2.4 in 1992), above the US level in 2016. Gidron (2026) reports that October 7 did not reduce it.

Support for the 2023 judicial overhaul was driven mainly by attachment to Netanyahu and hostility toward opponents (Gidron et al. 2025, AJPS). The 2015 campaign gains came almost entirely from within each bloc. In August 2022 only about 6% of voters planned to switch blocs, and an August 2026 Channel 12 poll put voters torn between the blocs at about 1.3%. National persuasion is therefore a thin, specific pool. Bloc outcomes depend mostly on three things: differential turnout, wasted votes below the threshold, and a few cross-pressured segments.

**Who is persuadable**
- **Traditional (masorti) non-religious Jews.** Only about 57% call themselves right-wing. In 2022 they voted roughly 46% Likud, 17% Yesh Atid and 14% National Unity.
- **Secular voters who backed Likud.** About 20% of secular voters, and about a third of Likud's electorate.
- **Druze.** About 90% vote for Zionist parties, and their choice among them is utilitarian and large: Blue and White went from 36% to 48% of the Druze vote within 2019.
- **Older Russian-speaking immigrants**, in part.

Haredi, national-religious and most Arab localities are close to zero persuasion targets for the Zionist change bloc. UTJ behaves as a "sect party", and national-religious voters became more radical between 2019 and 2022. The Mizrahi-Ashkenazi gap (25 points at locality level in 2022) mostly disappears once education and religiosity are controlled for. The model should predict locality bloc share from education, religiosity, socio-economic status and age, not from origin. Young Jewish adults are the most right-wing age group (73-75% identify as right-wing, against 46% of those 65 and over).

**Strategic voting.** Israeli voters are highly coalition-minded: 95% have coalition expectations. They desert parties they see as unlikely to govern, and switch to influence who forms the government. This mainly reshuffles votes inside a bloc, for example toward the leading change party, rather than adding to the bloc. Threshold losses were decisive in 2022: 8.7% of votes were wasted, about 300,000 of them from Meretz and Balad, which handed a near-tied vote a 64-seat majority. Consolidating sub-threshold change-leaning votes is a first-order lever.

**Leaders.** Personalisation is strong: party identification as the main reason for a vote fell to 13% by 2015. The closest precedent is Kadima in 2006, a security-credentialed centrist leader who drew 31% of 2003 Likud voters, mostly through personal pull. This gives an upper bound for Yashar's reach into soft-Likud localities.

**Turnout.** At locality level (2022, including double envelopes), development towns turned out 6-8 points below prediction and kibbutzim about 4 points below, while settlements were about 5 points above and Haredi share raised turnout. In 2022 right-leaning periphery towns raised turnout much more than centre-left cities (Dimona +6.9 points against Tel Aviv +0.3). In 2021 a turnout drop in right-wing strongholds hurt Likud.

**Security shocks.** Rocket and terror exposure shifts localities right by roughly 1-6 points. How this applies to the October 7 localities is uncertain, because a majority of the public also wants a state commission of inquiry.

**Caveats.** The shared web-search budget ran out before I could find the Kolot Nodedim (harelc) vote-transfer work, recent vote-transition tables or 2022 data on Russian-speaking voters. Those gaps are listed under open questions.

findings.claim: Elsewhere in advanced democracies, issue voting grew while social cleavages lost explanatory power. In Israel issue voting grew but cleavages kept structuring the vote. The reason is 'identity dilemmas' (territory and security, Jewish character of the state, religion-state) that fuse policy with group belonging. Analysis covers 1969-1996.
findings.quant: Longitudinal INES cleavage analysis 1969-1996; overall explanatory power of the vote models held up over the period (no single effect size in the abstract).
findings.authors: Michal Shamir; Asher Arian
findings.title: Collective Identity and Electoral Competition in Israel
findings.relevance: Theoretical basis for building locality baselines from group composition (religiosity, nationality, education, origin proxies) rather than treating localities as freely swinging. Swing potential should be concentrated where residents are cross-pressured across identity dimensions, e.g. secular or traditional voters who are hawkish on security but liberal on religion-state.

findings.claim: In the 2015 election Israeli left-right was 'captive' to the collective-identity cleavage. Left and right are defined by security, territory and Jewish-Arab identity, not by economics. The campaign tied the left to Arabs. A later INES-based chapter (Amitai 2025) cites this work for the point that economic attitudes do not line up with Israeli left-right.
findings.quant: No figures verified (I could not access the chapter text). Book chapter pp. 139-164.
findings.authors: Michal Shamir; Shira Dvir-Gvirsman; Raphael Ventura
findings.title: Taken Captive by the Collective Identity Cleavage: Left and Right in the 2015 Elections (in The Elections in Israel 2015, eds. Shamir & Rahat)
findings.relevance: Economic and cost-of-living messages are unlikely to move bloc identity by themselves. Change-bloc appeals in soft-right localities need to be framed in security and national-identity terms, which fits Eisenkot and Bennett. Do not use left-coded identity cues there.

findings.claim: INES 2022, Jewish voters. There is broad consensus on economic-social questions: about 65% prefer a social-democratic economy, and about 65% support civil marriage. Deep divides remain on the Palestinian conflict, religion in public life and Supreme Court powers, and the conflict and court items best predicted the 2022 vote. Ideological gaps between party electorates were stable over the decade. Likud voters sit in the middle: at least 35% take the opposite position to their religious and Haredi partners on religion-state and court powers, and they are split on civil marriage and weakening the court. They are hawkish and united with their bloc on security.
findings.quant: About 65% of Jews prefer socialist over capitalist economics; about 65% support civil marriage; at least 35% of Likud voters oppose their religious partners' positions on religion-state and court powers.
findings.authors: Yaniv Shapira (chapter in Rahat, Gidron & Shamir, eds.)
findings.title: Do We Agree, and on What? Ideological Cleavages and Public Opinion Trends in the 2022 Elections (Hebrew; in The Elections in Israel 2022)
findings.relevance: Identifies the persuadable sub-electorate: secular and traditional Likud voters who are cross-pressured on religion-state (Haredi draft, civil marriage) and on the judiciary. Locality persuasion scores should weight the estimated share of non-religious Likud voters. Message content: security credibility plus religion-state fairness, not territorial compromise.

findings.claim: INES 1992-2022. Ideological polarisation rose only modestly. Bimodality reached 0.52 in 2022, close to but below the 0.55 cutoff. The correlation between issue dimensions (excluding economics) rose from 0.32 to 0.6. Affective polarisation between the two main parties' voters more than doubled in 1992-1999 (2.4 to 5.3), eased in 2001-2009, then rose 180% from 2009 to an all-time high of 6.2 in 2022, above the US 2016 level of 4.7 on the same scale. It increasingly centres on Netanyahu himself.
findings.quant: Affective polarisation 2.4 (1992), 5.3 (1999), 6.2 (2022, +180% vs 2009); US 2016 = 4.7. Bimodality 0.52 (2022). Issue-constraint correlation 0.32 to 0.6.
findings.authors: Yair Amitai (chapter in Rahat, Gidron & Shamir, eds.)
findings.title: Political Polarization in Israel 1992-2022 (Hebrew; in The Elections in Israel 2022)
findings.relevance: Cross-bloc persuasion elasticities should be small. Persuasion effort belongs only in localities with large low-affect, weakly partisan segments, such as traditional non-religious voters, Druze and older Russian-speaking immigrants. Elsewhere, campaign value comes from turnout.

findings.claim: Gidron reports that the war after October 7 did not reduce domestic partisan hostility, contrary to rally-effect expectations. Affective polarisation has fluctuated around the 2022 peak, and partisan animosity has proved more persistent than expected. His 10-wave Israel Polarization Panel (2019-2021, four elections) shows party-specific polarisation moving with electoral performance and coalition composition.
findings.quant: Qualitative: post-October 7 polarisation is at roughly 2022-peak levels. The IPP has 10 panel waves across 4 elections.
findings.authors: Noam Gidron (interview by Bruno Cousin); dataset: Gidron, Sheffer & Mor (Electoral Studies 80:102512, 2022)
findings.title: On Democratic Backsliding in Israel (interview)
findings.venue: Books and Ideas / La Vie des idées
findings.relevance: Do not assume a post-October 7 thaw that makes Likud voters broadly persuadable. Keep a 2022-calibrated low cross-bloc elasticity. Ad-hoc swing should be driven by segment composition, not a uniform national post-war shift.

findings.claim: A panel surveyed the same people in January 2023 (before the overhaul) and April 2023 (after). Among coalition voters, support for the judicial overhaul was best explained by prior attachment to Netanyahu and animosity toward opposition parties. Majoritarian views and bad experiences with the legal system mattered more weakly, and populist attitudes not at all.
findings.quant: Abstract reports no effect sizes. Panel waves in January and April 2023.
findings.authors: Noam Gidron; Yotam Margalit; Lior Sheffer; Itamar Yakir
findings.title: Why Masses Support Democratic Backsliding
findings.relevance: The persuadable coalition voters are those with weak personal attachment to Netanyahu and low out-party hostility, typically less ideological traditional and secular Likud voters. Attack messaging that raises animosity hardens rather than converts. In persuasion localities, use contrast on competence and responsibility, not identity attacks.

findings.claim: Across seven Israeli election studies, a natural experiment shows that higher salience of electoral competition increases affective polarisation. A survey experiment after the September 2019 election shows that priming a unity government (cooperation between rival parties) increases tolerance across party lines.
findings.quant: Causal direction established; abstract gives no magnitudes.
findings.authors: Lotem Bassan-Nygate; Chagai M. Weiss
findings.title: Party Competition and Cooperation Shape Affective Polarization: Evidence from Natural and Survey Experiments in Israel
findings.relevance: In soft-right persuasion localities, framing the change bloc as broad and inclusive of the centre-right, rather than 'us against them', should lower resistance. In base-mobilisation localities, competitive framing can drive turnout. Messaging should differ by locality type.

findings.claim: In 2015 both Likud and the Zionist Union gained compared with 2013, but almost all their gains came from parties in their own bloc. Identity-based campaigns targeted voters inside each bloc and sharpened the boundaries between blocs.
findings.quant: Qualitative: almost all big-party gains came from within the bloc.
findings.authors: Gideon Rahat; Reuven Y. Hazan; Pazit Ben-Nun Bloom
findings.title: Stable Blocs and Multiple Identities: The 2015 Elections in Israel
findings.relevance: Most party-level volatility in locality results reshuffles votes inside a bloc. Swing indices should be computed on bloc shares (change vs Netanyahu vs Arab), not party shares. Otherwise localities churning between Likud and Otzma, or Yesh Atid and National Unity, look falsely swingy.

findings.claim: INES 1969-2006 shows growing dealignment. Instability between parties within blocs rose faster than instability between blocs. Individual-level switching reached 63% in 2006 (50% in the 1977 realignment), and aggregate party volatility hit a record 42.7%. Closeness to a party fell from 64% (1996) to 54% (2006). Kadima, a centrist party led by former Likud leader Sharon, drew 42% of its vote from 2003 Likud voters, 23% from Labor and 17% from Shinui. 31% of 2003 Likud voters ended up voting Kadima, after 53% said they would in December 2005. More than half of the Likud-to-Kadima switchers cited personal support for Sharon.
findings.quant: Individual switching 63% (2006); party volatility 42.7%; 31% of 2003 Likud voters voted Kadima (53% intended in December 2005); 42% of Kadima vote from ex-Likud; more than 50% of Likud switchers cited Sharon personally; 'very close' to a party 37% to 24% (1996 to 2006).
findings.authors: Michal Shamir; Raphael Ventura; Asher Arian; Orit Kedar
findings.title: Kadima - Forward in a Dealigned Party System (in The Elections in Israel 2006)
findings.relevance: Best Israeli precedent for a security-credentialed centrist leader (Eisenkot / Yashar) pulling soft-Likud voters through leader pull. It gives an upper bound of roughly 30% of soft-Likud voters at a high-water mark, with fade-out of about 40% between intention and vote. Expect such gains to concentrate in secular and traditional Likud localities, and discount poll-stage intentions.

findings.claim: August 2022 (n=754). About half of respondents intended to repeat their 2021 vote, about a quarter were undecided, and only 6% planned to switch blocs. Among Jews, 78% of then-opposition (Netanyahu-bloc) voters planned to repeat their vote, against 43.5% of then-coalition (Bennett-Lapid) voters. 10% of coalition voters, mostly 2021 Yamina voters, planned to move to the Netanyahu bloc; only 4% moved the other way. Among Arab voters, 15% of Ra'am's 2021 voters planned to vote Joint List, against 1% the other way.
findings.quant: Bloc switchers 6%; change-to-Netanyahu 10% of change voters vs 4% reverse; Netanyahu-bloc repeat rate 78% vs 43.5%; Ra'am to Joint List 15%.
findings.authors: Israel Democracy Institute (Viterbi Center, Israeli Voice Index)
findings.title: Only Half of Israelis Intend to Repeat Their 2021 Vote
findings.relevance: Calibrates the cross-bloc pool at a few percent. Shows that the soft-right voters inside a change coalition (Yamina 2021) are the least loyal. The 2026 Together list (Bennett) faces the same retention risk: localities with high 2021 Yamina and New Hope shares need retention campaigning.

findings.claim: An August 2026 policy brief cites a Channel 12 poll. Only about 1.3% of respondents were undecided between the Netanyahu bloc and the change bloc, roughly 90,000 voters or about 2 seats. 9.8% were undecided overall, mostly between parties inside one bloc. The three-way seat map (about 50 Netanyahu coalition / 60 opposition / 10 Arab) had held for more than three years.
findings.quant: 1.3% torn between blocs (~90k voters, ~2 seats); 9.8% undecided overall.
findings.authors: Yael Patir (J Street), citing a Channel 12 poll
findings.title: Israeli Election Update: A Frozen Political Map - But No Clear Government
findings.relevance: Supports putting most of the targeting weight on turnout and threshold consolidation, with persuasion confined to small, identifiable segments. I could not open the page directly (it returned 404); figures come from search-result summaries.

findings.topic: 2022 outcome: differential turnout and Yamina collapse
findings.claim: From 2021 to 2022 the Netanyahu bloc rose from 48.3% to 49.6%, the centre-left plus right-wing anti-Netanyahu bloc fell from 41.5% to 38.3%, and Arab parties rose from 8.6% to 10.8%. Yamina-Jewish Home lost more than 80% of its 2021 voters, mostly to Religious Zionism-Otzma (5.1% to 10.8%). Turnout rose from 67.4% to 70.6%, and much more in right-leaning towns: Dimona +6.9, Beersheba +4.6, Ashkelon +3.2 points, against about +0.3-0.4 in Tel Aviv, Givatayim and Herzliya. The share of Arab votes going to Zionist parties fell from 52.3% (1992) to 14.2% (2022).
findings.quant: Bloc shares 48.3 to 49.6 / 41.5 to 38.3 / 8.6 to 10.8; turnout +3.2 points nationally; periphery right towns +3 to +7 points vs centre-left cities +0.3 to 0.4; Yamina retained under 20%.
findings.authors: Ori Wertman; Meir Elran
findings.title: The Israeli Electorate from the Perspective of the 2022 Elections (INSS Insight 1664)
findings.relevance: Centre-left strongholds sit at a turnout ceiling, while right-leaning periphery cities have large mobilisation swings. The model needs locality-specific turnout elasticities. The change bloc's realistic turnout gains are in mid-turnout mixed localities, and in persuading soft-right periphery voters rather than out-mobilising them. When a soft-right party collapses, its voters went right in 2022, not to the centre.

findings.claim: In March 2021 turnout fell across the country compared with 2020, and the fall was larger in religious and right-wing strongholds. That weakened Likud considerably.
findings.quant: Qualitative in text; figures are in slides I could not read.
findings.authors: Ofer Kenig (IDI)
findings.title: Voting Patterns in Knesset Elections 2021 Vs. 2020
findings.relevance: Together with the 2022 rebound (D1-F12), this shows turnout in Likud strongholds swings with enthusiasm and accounts for several seats. Model locality turnout as a stochastic component that differs by bloc lean. In soft-Likud localities, weakening attachment to Netanyahu can reduce net Netanyahu-bloc votes even without conversion.

findings.claim: Pooled IDI surveys (20 surveys, 10,694 Jewish voters, November 2022-October 2023). Share voting for the parties that formed the coalition: Haredim 97%, national-religious 80%, traditional 66.5%. 74% of secular voters backed the opposition. Traditional non-religious voters: Likud 46, Yesh Atid 17, National Unity 14, Shas+UTJ 2. Traditional-religious: Likud 47, RZP-Otzma 17, Shas 10. Secular: Yesh Atid 39, Likud 20, Labor+Meretz 16, National Unity 13. National-religious: RZP-Otzma 45, Likud 22.5. From 2021 to 2022 among traditional voters: Likud 39 to 46.5, RZP-Otzma 4 to 14, National Unity 18 to 12.5.
findings.quant: Coalition share: Haredi 97%, national-religious 80%, traditional 66.5%; secular 74% opposition. Traditional non-religious: Likud 46 / Yesh Atid 17 / National Unity 14. Secular Likud 20%.
findings.authors: Ariel Finkelstein (IDI)
findings.title: Voting Patterns of Jews in the 2022 Elections by Religious Self-Definition
findings.relevance: Core calibration for segment persuadability. The traditional non-religious segment is the genuine swing group: it split roughly 46/31 between Likud and change parties and moved by double digits between 2021 and 2022. Secular Likud voters come second. Locality persuasion score should rise with the estimated share of traditional non-religious plus secular-right voters (CBS religiosity and Social Survey proxies).

findings.claim: Israeli Democracy Index 2022, Jews. 62% identify as right, 24% centre, 11% left, and the right share has risen in every age group over 20 years. Right-wing identification by age: 18-24 73%, 25-34 75%, 35-44 62%, 45-54 53%, 55-64 52%, 65+ 46%. By religiosity (right/centre/left): Haredim 74.5/12/4, national-religious 82/10/4, traditional 57/26/11, secular 32/32/30.
findings.quant: Right ID 62% (Jews); 18-24 73% vs 65+ 46%; traditional 26% centre (largest centre share of any religious group besides secular).
findings.authors: Israel Democracy Institute (Israeli Democracy Index 2022)
findings.title: The Israeli Democracy Index 2022 - Selected Findings
findings.relevance: Localities with young age structures lean right. Youth turnout drives yield little for the change bloc except in secular and university localities. Traditional voters hold the largest movable centre. Add age structure as a covariate for both bloc lean and persuasion yield.

findings.claim: Based on INES March 2021 data (n=1,816): 47% of 'not-so-religious' masortim and 55% of 'religious' masortim voted Likud. The page reports 39% and 22% respectively for Blue and White, which looks inconsistent with Blue and White's 2021 size and may come from a different wave. Composition of Likud voters: secular 34%, masorti non-religious 30%, masorti-religious 18%. The author attributes masorti over-representation in Likud mainly to education and SES gaps, not ethnicity.
findings.quant: Likud 47% (masorti non-religious) / 55% (masorti-religious); Likud electorate 34% secular, 30% masorti non-religious.
findings.authors: Gabriel Abensour (JPPI)
findings.title: Masortim and Masortiyut in Israel - Identity and Education
findings.relevance: About two-thirds of Likud's vote comes from secular and non-religious masorti voters, the cross-pressured groups. Localities where Likud dominates among non-religious residents (many development towns and peripheral cities) are the persuasion battleground, not localities where Likud's vote is religious.

findings.claim: Covers 440 small Jewish localities classified by most common surnames, plus urban statistical areas, across ten elections (2003-2022). In 2022 the right bloc won about 61% in Mizrahi localities against about 36% in Ashkenazi localities, a gap of about 25 points. The gap was only about 5 points in 2006, and 2022's was five times 2006 and more than twice 2009. In all ten elections the gap disappears or shrinks considerably once education and religiosity are controlled for. Right-bloc vote falls with education, income and median age. Higher education was neutral between blocs in 2003-2013 but became strongly pro-centre-left over the last six cycles.
findings.quant: Raw origin gap about 25 points (2022) vs about 5 points (2006). Education coefficient negative and sizable since 2015. Locality sample matches the national right-bloc share within 1 point.
findings.authors: Momi Dahan
findings.title: Voting Gap by Origin (CESifo Working Paper 10857; later Israel Economic Review 2025)
findings.venue: CESifo / Bank of Israel Israel Economic Review
findings.relevance: Model locality bloc share with education, religiosity, income and age rather than origin. The volatility of the origin gap means Mizrahi-majority localities are not fixed and the 2022 peak may partly revert. Education is the strongest secular predictor of change-bloc support, so use it for both baseline and persuasion weighting.

findings.claim: Covers all 1,215 localities with polling stations in 2022, the first such study to include double-envelope votes assigned to localities. Turnout was 73.0% in Jewish and mixed localities and 56.0% in Arab localities. Jewish-locality regression: SES +0.53 points per index unit; periphery not significant; development towns −6.3 points; kibbutzim −4.3; Judea and Samaria +4.9; Haredi share +0.057 points per percentage point; size negative. Arab localities: SES +1.8, centrality +2.2 per unit, size +1.75. All-locality model: Arab localities −26.3 points, development towns −7.8 points. The centre-periphery gap among Jewish localities (without double envelopes) widened from 2.5 points (April 2019) to 3.6 (September 2019) to 4.4 (2022). Among Arab localities the gap ranged 14-26 points with no trend.
findings.quant: Jewish 73.0% vs Arab 56.0%; development towns −6.3 points; kibbutzim −4.3; settlements +4.9; Arab −26.3; adjusted R² 0.16 Jewish, 0.16 Arab, 0.60 all.
findings.authors: Nir Atmor (chapter in Rahat, Gidron & Shamir, eds.)
findings.title: Who Flocked to the Polls? Turnout in the 2022 Elections (Hebrew; in The Elections in Israel 2022)
findings.relevance: Gives direct coefficients for a turnout-headroom model. Development towns have structural headroom but lean right. Kibbutzim, change-bloc strongholds, turn out about 4 points below prediction: a high-yield change-bloc mobilisation target. Settlements and Haredi localities are already saturated. Arab turnout depends on SES, centrality and size.

findings.claim: Special 'double-envelope' votes (soldiers, police, diplomats and others voting away from their assigned station) grew substantially over the past decade. Assigning them to localities, using data obtained by petitioning the Central Elections Committee, changes measured turnout gaps across localities and groups. In the companion 2022 locality data, Jewish and mixed localities had 5,850,403 eligible voters, 3,832,892 regular votes and 438,034 double envelopes. Arab localities had 938,401 eligible, 498,894 regular votes and 26,933 double envelopes.
findings.quant: Double envelopes about 7.5% of eligible voters (about 10% of votes) in Jewish localities vs about 2.9% of eligible in Arab localities (2022).
findings.authors: Nir Atmor; Chen Friedberg; Ofer Kenig
findings.title: Special votes and voter turnout in Israel's 2022 elections
findings.relevance: Our CEC kalpi-level data understate turnout in young and soldier-heavy Jewish localities by several points. Before computing turnout headroom, add a locality-level double-envelope correction (larger for young, settlement and periphery localities). Otherwise the model will falsely flag them as low-turnout opportunities.

findings.claim: National-religious: the religious public radicalised between 2019 and 2022 on almost every INES measure. Opposition to a Palestinian state rose from 76% to 86%, right self-placement increased, and support for a full-right coalition rose from 61% (2019) to 85% (2021). Yamina voters moved to RZP-Otzma. Moderate religious-Zionists may drift to non-sectoral parties. UTJ is a 'sect party' with an unusually loyal core. Its vote grew about 4% a year in 1992-2022 (4.4% falling to 3.7%), roughly the growth of the Ashkenazi Haredi electorate. 8-14% of UTJ voters are non-Haredi, and about 10% of Ashkenazi Haredim sometimes vote elsewhere.
findings.quant: Religious opposition to a Palestinian state 76% to 86% (2019 to 2022); full-right coalition preference 61% to 85%; UTJ vote growth about 3.7-4.4% a year; dynamic fringe 8-14%.
findings.authors: Michael Freedman; Gilad Malach (chapters in Rahat, Gidron & Shamir, eds.)
findings.title: From Bennett to Ben Gvir: Religious-Zionist Voting 2019-2022; Does UTJ's Growth Match Haredi Population Growth? (Hebrew; in The Elections in Israel 2022)
findings.relevance: Set persuasion weight near zero for Haredi and national-religious localities and model their turnout as high and stable. Apply a structural drift toward the Netanyahu bloc of about +0.15-0.2 points of national vote a year from Haredi growth. A small moderate religious-Zionist pool exists for Bennett's list, mainly in mixed religious-secular suburbs, not religious towns.

findings.claim: Russian speakers are about 15% of Israel's population (about 900,000), worth roughly 16-17 seats in potential but about 14 at actual (below-average) turnout. Yisrael Beytenu has been the core party, with immigrant voters giving it most of its strength. Likud has drawn about 3-4 seats from them, and Blue and White about 2 in April 2019. By generation: adult 1990s immigrants are to the right of native-born Israelis, those who arrived as teenagers lean centrist, and the Israeli-born second generation resembles native voters. 50-60% are secular.
findings.quant: About 15% of population; about 14 seats at actual turnout vs 16-17 potential; Likud about 3-4 seats; Blue and White about 2 seats (April 2019).
findings.authors: Izabella Tabarovsky (Kennan Institute), citing Ze'ev Khanin and Yuri Teper
findings.title: Russian-Speaking Israelis Go to the Polls
findings.venue: Wilson Center Kennan Institute (The Russia File)
findings.relevance: With Yisrael Beytenu in the change bloc, FSU-heavy localities (e.g. Ashdod, Ashkelon, Bat Yam, Nof HaGalil, Karmiel, Kiryat Yam, Ma'alot, Ariel) combine below-average turnout (headroom) with a secular, security-hawkish profile open to religion-state messaging. They are high-value for both turnout and persuasion. Weight by the share of adult 1990s immigrants. 2022 distribution not verified.

findings.claim: Druze voting is mainly utilitarian: support goes to parties expected to govern, or with a local or family candidate who can deliver benefits. Estimated Druze vote in Druze localities (2015 / April 2019 / September 2019): Yisrael Beytenu 23.8/12.6/18.8; Blue and White not running/36.0/47.8; Likud 7.8/11.1/9.6; Kulanu 18.4 (2015); Meretz 2.0/15.8/3.2. Turnout 57.7/60.1/54.5. Druze kept backing parties that passed the Nation-State Law despite opposing it.
findings.quant: Blue and White +11.8 points within 5 months (36.0 to 47.8); Yisrael Beytenu swings of ±6-11 points; turnout 54-60%.
findings.authors: Salim Brake
findings.title: The Druze Vote for the Twentieth, Twenty-First, and Twenty-Second Knesset Elections
findings.venue: Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University (Bayan)
findings.relevance: Druze localities (e.g. Daliyat al-Karmel, Yarka, Isfiya, Beit Jann, Maghar, Julis, Hurfeish) are true swing localities between the Netanyahu bloc and Zionist change parties. They have very high party volatility and below-average turnout, and respond to realistic Druze candidates and coalition prospects. Give them high persuasion and turnout weights. Candidate placement and local notables matter more than national messaging.

findings.claim: Arab and Druze turnout was 53.2% in 2022 (decade average 55.9%; range 44.6% in 2021 to 64.8% in 2020). Arab lists took 85.8% of Arab votes and Jewish parties 14.3% (under 2 seats): National Unity 3.2% (about 11k of its 15k votes from Druze), Meretz 2.7%, Likud 2.2%, Yisrael Beytenu 2.0%, Yesh Atid 1.7%. Zionist parties won about 90% in Druze towns. Ra'am won 66.8% in northern Bedouin localities and 73.9% in the Negev. Northern Triangle turnout was 46.2% against 60.8% in the southern Triangle. Strong local-candidate effects. Fragmentation into three lists raised turnout in 2022, unlike earlier cycles.
findings.quant: Turnout 53.2% (Arab and Druze); Jewish-party share 14.3%; Druze towns about 90% Zionist; Ra'am 66.8% northern Bedouin and 73.9% Negev; Triangle 46.2% vs 60.8%.
findings.authors: Arik Rudnitzky
findings.title: Summary of the 25th Knesset election results in Arab society (Bayan 28)
findings.venue: Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Outside Druze localities, Arab localities offer little direct vote for the Zionist change bloc. Their turnout still matters for the bloc arithmetic, through Ra'am and Joint List seats and threshold risk. Treat Arab localities as a separate turnout-only module and Druze localities as a Zionist-party swing module. Arab turnout is highly volatile (SD about 8 points) and sensitive to list configuration and local candidates.

findings.claim: Uses the 2006 Israeli election. Voters who see their preferred party as unlikely to join the coalition often desert it for the lesser evil among viable partners. The effect holds after controlling for ideological and coalition preferences. 95% of respondents gave coalition expectations. The effect was found for the main parties (Labor, Likud) but not for smaller or sectoral parties (Meretz, Shas, Yisrael Beytenu, NRP).
findings.quant: 95% of respondents coalition-attentive; perceived probability of Kadima-Labor coalition 0.62. Effect significant for Labor and Likud only.
findings.authors: Matias A. Bargsted; Orit Kedar
findings.title: Coalition-Targeted Duvergerian Voting: How Expectations Affect Voter Choice under Proportional Representation
findings.relevance: Perceived viability of a change government affects consolidation among mainstream voters but barely moves sectoral party voters. Messaging about a credible path to 61 matters in centre-right localities. Expect strategic flows between Yashar, Together and Likud, but not out of Shas or UTJ.

findings.topic: formateur optimisation / vote switching in repeat elections
findings.claim: A three-wave online panel in Israel during the 2019-2020 repeat elections. Voters switched to influence who would become the next formateur, and abandoned parties they expected to be left out of the next coalition. The effect of coalition expectations on switching was stronger when voters saw the race between potential formateurs as close.
findings.quant: Abstract reports no effect sizes; 3 panel waves (2019-2020).
findings.authors: Liran Harsgor; Reut Itzkovitch-Malka; Or Tuttnauer
findings.title: Do coalition and formateur expectations affect vote switching?
findings.relevance: With Yashar and Likud close for largest party, 'largest party gets the mandate' messaging can drive within-bloc consolidation to Yashar. This adds no bloc seats, but can matter for who is tasked with forming the government. Model a consolidation term that grows with perceived closeness, concentrated in localities with fragmented change-bloc votes.

findings.claim: Because coalition bargaining dilutes each party's policy influence, outcome-oriented voters sometimes support parties more extreme than themselves to pull the final coalition policy toward their ideal. This reconciles proximity and directional voting. Tested on four parliamentary democracies; I could not confirm whether Israel is among them.
findings.quant: No magnitudes verified (scanned PDF unreadable).
findings.authors: Orit Kedar
findings.title: When Moderate Voters Prefer Extreme Parties: Policy Balancing in Parliamentary Elections
findings.relevance: Helps explain why some moderate right voters chose Otzma or RZP, and why some centre-left voters choose the Democrats: both are within-bloc balancing. This again argues for bloc-level swing metrics. Persuading balancing voters across blocs is unlikely.

findings.claim: Compares vote intentions in FPTP or majoritarian contests (US, Mexico, Britain, Israeli PM races) and PR contests (Israel, Netherlands). A substantial share of voters desert their most preferred party, with similar patterns across systems. Smaller parties consistently lose votes to larger ones. Tactical voting is more common under PR because PR has more small parties.
findings.quant: No percentages extracted (PDF unavailable); smaller parties lost votes in every election studied.
findings.authors: Paul R. Abramson; John H. Aldrich; André Blais; Matthew Diamond; Abraham Diskin; Indridi H. Indridason; Daniel J. Lee; Renan Levine
findings.title: Comparing Strategic Voting Under FPTP and PR
findings.relevance: Sub-threshold lists (Reservists about 1.6%, Blue and White about 1%) should lose votes in the final stretch. Where those votes go is a key swing component. Localities where these lists poll strongest are priority targets for consolidation messaging.

findings.claim: In 2022 about 8.7% of votes were wasted, an all-time high, against 0.8% and 1.5% in the two previous elections and 5-6% in 1992 and 1999. Meretz and Balad, both outside the Netanyahu bloc, wasted about 300,000 votes. The two blocs won nearly identical vote totals, but the threshold's 'knockout effect' gave Netanyahu's camp 64 seats.
findings.quant: Wasted 8.7% (2022) vs 0.8-1.5% (2020-2021); about 300k anti-Netanyahu votes lost.
findings.authors: Assaf Shapira (IDI)
findings.title: Wasted Votes, the Electoral Threshold, and the Relationship between Them
findings.relevance: Threshold management can outweigh all locality persuasion combined. The model's 'impact' metric should include each locality's contribution to sub-threshold change-leaning lists and to marginal parties near 3.25%. Priority goes to persuading voters in localities where B&W or Reservists are strong to consolidate into viable change lists.

findings.claim: INES 1977-2015, main reason for vote choice. Party identification fell from 28-33% (1977-1988) to 13.1% in 2015. The party leader was the main reason for 19.2% in 2015. The ratio of party to personal reasons fell from 1.77 (1977) to 0.45 (2015). Issue positions stayed the plurality (about 50-64%).
findings.quant: Party-ID motive 27.9% (1977) to 13.1% (2015); leader motive 19.2% (2015); party:personal ratio 1.77 to 0.45.
findings.authors: Gideon Rahat
findings.title: The Decline of the Group and the Rise of the Star(s): From Party Politics to Personal Politics (IDI Policy Paper 145, Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Leader-centred campaigning (an Eisenkot or Bennett versus Netanyahu head-to-head) and in-person leader visits are justified tools. Leader visits should be allocated to high-persuasion localities. Track leader favourability, not only party vote, in locality polling.

findings.claim: Using the expanding range of Gaza rockets as exogenous variation (elections 1999-2009), localities inside rocket range showed a right-wing vote share about 2-6 points higher. A later working paper (Elster 2017, Hebrew University) uses rocket-damage claims for 1999-2015. It finds an extra 1,000 claims in a locality raises right-bloc share by about 4 points, driven by actual hits rather than mere threat, and stronger for recent, first-time and nearby attacks.
findings.quant: +2 to +6 points right vote within rocket range; about +4 points per 1,000 damage claims (Elster).
findings.authors: Anna Getmansky; Thomas Zeitzoff
findings.title: Terrorism and Voting: The Effect of Rocket Threat on Voting in Israeli Elections
findings.relevance: Post-2023 war exposure (Gaza envelope, the north, central-Israel missile hits) is a locality covariate expected to shift right. Apply a prior of about +2 to +4 points to the Netanyahu bloc in heavily hit localities, with wide uncertainty because of blame for October 7 (see D1-F33).

findings.topic: security shocks and locality vote (terror attacks)
findings.claim: A terror attack in a locality within three months of an election raises that locality's right-bloc share of the two-bloc vote by 1.35 points. Fatalities also have effects beyond the attacked locality, and these are stronger closer to the election. In left-leaning localities, local fatalities increase right support, while fatalities elsewhere increase left support.
findings.quant: +1.35 points right-bloc per local attack within 3 months of the election.
findings.authors: Claude Berrebi; Esteban F. Klor
findings.title: Are Voters Sensitive to Terrorism? Direct Evidence from the Israeli Electorate
findings.relevance: Late-campaign security incidents can shift exposed localities by about 1-2 points. Build a scenario layer for election-eve shocks, and keep rapid-response capacity in exposed swing localities.

findings.claim: Survey of 31 December 2024-6 January 2025 (1,000 Jews, 202 Arabs). Only 8.5% named the overhaul the government's top priority, against 40.5% security and 34% cost of living. 55% opposed the overhaul and 36.5% supported it (Jews 50.5% opposed). 61% said now is not the time. Among right-wing Jews, 40% said now is not the time and 30% agreed it over-concentrates power. 59% of the right cited concern for national unity.
findings.quant: Overhaul top priority 8.5%; oppose 55% vs support 36.5%; right 'not the time' 40%; right 'over-concentration' 30%.
findings.authors: Anat Thon Ashkenazy (IDI Center for Democratic Values and Institutions / Viterbi Center)
findings.title: Special Survey: Public Opinion on the Judicial Overhaul (January 2025)
findings.relevance: For soft-right persuadables, the overhaul is a low-salience issue, though roughly 30-40% of the right is cross-pressured on it. Lead persuasion in right-leaning swing localities with security competence, cost of living and national unity, and use democracy and judiciary themes for base mobilisation.

findings.claim: IDI Israeli Voice Index, December 2025. 55.1% favour a state commission of inquiry into October 7 (Jews 53.9%), against 22.1% for a government-appointed committee. Jewish respondents on a government relying on Ra'am if the blocs tie: 12.5% would support it in any case, 13.9% only if there is no other option, 7.7% only with external support, and 57.8% would not.
findings.quant: State commission of inquiry 55%; Jewish support for a Ra'am-reliant government 12.5% unconditional, about 34% under some condition; 57.8% opposed.
findings.authors: Israel Democracy Institute (Viterbi Center)
findings.title: Israeli Voice Index - December 2025 (data)
findings.relevance: A state commission of inquiry is a majority wedge position that reaches beyond the change base, useful in swing localities. Dependence on Ra'am is a liability among Jewish swing voters, so messaging in soft-right localities should stress a Zionist majority path. This matters given our 19% Ra'am-dependent scenario.

findings.claim: Agam Labs (Hebrew University; Nimrod Nir) ran a panel of about 4,000 adults from August 2023 and roughly every 10 days from 9 October 2023 to May 2024. Jewish right-wing identification moved from about 58% to about 60%, left from 17% to 13%, and centre from 25% to about 27%. The shift was mainly on security and Palestinian questions rather than broad ideology, and partly reversed during the war.
findings.quant: Right about 58 to 60%; left 17 to 13%; centre 25 to 27% (Jews, August 2023 to May 2024); about 4 points margin per round.
findings.authors: Agam Labs (Nimrod Nir), as reported by JNS
findings.title: Israeli Jews more right-wing after Oct. 7
findings.venue: JNS (news report of an academic panel)
findings.relevance: Identity labels moved modestly right, so change-bloc lists led by security figures need to win voters who call themselves right or centre. Locality persuasion targeting should not exclude right-identifying non-religious voters. Not peer-reviewed.

parameters.name: cross_bloc_switch_pool_jewish
parameters.value: 3% of Jewish voters nationally are realistically movable between the Netanyahu and change blocs
parameters.basis: D1-F10: 6% planned to switch blocs in August 2022. D1-F11: 1.3% torn between blocs in August 2026. D1-F08: 2015 gains almost all within bloc. D1-F04 and D1-F05: polarisation at a record high and not reduced after October 7. Distribute the pool across localities by segment composition (see segment weights), not uniformly.

parameters.name: segment_persuadability_weights (relative propensity to cross blocs)
parameters.value: masorti non-religious 1.00; secular right-identifying / secular Likud 0.75; Druze (among Zionist parties) 0.80; FSU adult 1990s immigrants 0.60; masorti-religious 0.40; Israeli-born FSU 0.40; national-religious 0.10; Haredi 0.02; Arab Muslim/Christian (to Zionist change parties) 0.05; secular centre-left 0.05 (turnout target, not persuasion)
parameters.basis: D1-F14: traditional non-religious split Likud 46 / change parties about 31 and moved double digits 2021 to 2022; secular Likud 20%. D1-F15: traditional 26% centre. D1-F16: secular plus masorti non-religious about 64% of Likud voters. D1-F22: Druze swings ±10-12 points. D1-F21: FSU generational gradient. D1-F20: sectoral closure. D1-F23: 14% Arab vote to Jewish parties. Weights are an expert synthesis, not estimated coefficients.

parameters.name: max_persuasion_effect_per_locality
parameters.value: 1.0 pp change in bloc share in the most persuadable localities from a full campaign push
parameters.basis: Small pool (D1-F10, D1-F11), high affective polarisation (D1-F04, D1-F05), identity-anchored camps (D1-F06). Judgment; cross-check against the campaign-effects desk.

parameters.name: turnout_structural_deviation_coefficients (Jewish localities, 2022, incl. double envelopes)
parameters.value: development town −6.3 pp; kibbutz −4.3 pp; Judea & Samaria +4.9 pp; Haredi share +0.057 pp per pp; SES +0.53 pp per SES index unit; periphery n.s.
parameters.range: development town −4.7 to −7.8; kibbutz −3.2 to −5.4; settlements +3.4 to +6.4 (about ±2 SE)
parameters.basis: D1-F18 (Atmor 2025, N=1,069 Jewish/mixed localities). Use residual (actual minus predicted) turnout as headroom. Kibbutzim are change-bloc strongholds below predicted turnout.

parameters.name: arab_locality_turnout_model
parameters.value: baseline 53% (2022); election-to-election SD about 8 pp; +2.2 pp per centrality unit, +1.8 per SES unit, +1.75 per normalised size
parameters.basis: D1-F23 (Rudnitzky: 49.2, 59.2, 64.8, 44.6, 53.2) and D1-F18 (Arab model). Jewish-locality turnout SD across the same cycle is about 2 pp.

parameters.name: double_envelope_correction
parameters.value: add about 7.5% of eligible voters (about 10% of valid votes) to kalpi-based turnout in Jewish localities and about 2.9% in Arab localities, weighted toward young, settlement and periphery localities
parameters.range: Jewish 5-12% of eligible depending on age structure
parameters.basis: D1-F19 and the D1-F18 table (438,034 double envelopes for 5.85M eligible in Jewish/mixed localities; 26,933 for 0.94M in Arab localities, 2022).

parameters.name: security_exposure_shift
parameters.value: +3 pp to the Netanyahu bloc in localities with heavy rocket or missile damage or attacks; +1.35 pp per local attack within 3 months of election day
parameters.range: 0 to +6 pp (for October 7 border communities allow −2 to +4 because of blame effects)
parameters.basis: D1-F30 (+2 to +6 pp; Elster about +4 pp per 1,000 claims) and D1-F31 (+1.35 pp). Uncertainty widened by majority support for a state commission of inquiry (D1-F33).

parameters.name: origin_vs_education_religiosity
parameters.value: origin (Mizrahi share) coefficient ≈ 0 after controls; education coefficient strongly negative for Netanyahu-bloc share since 2015; religiosity strongly positive (excluding Haredi parties)
parameters.basis: D1-F17 (Dahan): 2022 right bloc 61% Mizrahi vs 36% Ashkenazi localities; the gap mostly vanishes with education and religiosity controls.

parameters.name: age_structure_effect
parameters.value: right identification 73-75% among 18-34 vs 46% among 65+; persuasion yield of young voters × 0.6 except in secular or university localities (× 1.0)

parameters.name: leader_pull_upper_bound
parameters.value: up to 15% of soft-Likud (non-religious) voters attracted by a security-credentialed centrist leader at election day
parameters.basis: D1-F09: Kadima drew 31% of 2003 Likud voters in 2006, after 53% intended in December, so about 40% fade. D1-F29: leader is the main motive for about 19% of voters. Current polarisation (D1-F04) argues for a lower central value than 2006.

parameters.name: sub_threshold_consolidation_rate
parameters.value: 40% of change-leaning votes for sub-threshold lists (Blue and White, Reservists) can be moved to viable change lists by consolidation messaging
parameters.basis: D1-F27 (small parties lose votes to large ones, more under PR), D1-F24 (coalition-attentive voters), D1-F28 (8.7% wasted in 2022 decided the majority). Judgment.

parameters.name: within_bloc_formateur_consolidation
parameters.value: 2-4 seats shift toward the leading change party (no net bloc change) when the largest-party race is seen as close
parameters.basis: D1-F25 (formateur optimisation, moderated by perceived competition) and D1-F24. Judgment; affects who forms the government, not the bloc total.

parameters.name: druze_locality_parameters
parameters.value: Zionist-party share about 90%; turnout about 55%; party volatility between consecutive elections up to ±12 pp
parameters.basis: D1-F22 (Brake: Blue and White 36.0 to 47.8; turnout 57.7/60.1/54.5) and D1-F23 (about 90% Zionist in 2022; National Unity about 11k Druze votes).

parameters.name: fsu_turnout_gap
parameters.value: −8 pp turnout relative to the Jewish average for adult 1990s FSU immigrants
parameters.basis: Derived from D1-F21 (about 14 seats at actual turnout vs 16-17 potential, roughly 85% relative turnout). Low confidence; verify with polling-station data in FSU-heavy neighbourhoods.

parameters.name: turnout_elasticity_by_bloc_lean
parameters.value: right-leaning periphery cities: mobilisation swing 3-7 pp between elections; centre-left strongholds 0.3-1 pp (ceiling)
parameters.basis: D1-F12 (2022: Dimona +6.9, Beersheba +4.6, Ashkelon +3.2 vs Tel Aviv, Givatayim, Herzliya +0.3-0.4) and D1-F13 (2021 drop concentrated in right and religious strongholds).

parameters.name: haredi_structural_drift
parameters.value: +0.15 to +0.2 pp a year of national vote share to Haredi parties from demographic growth
parameters.basis: D1-F20 (UTJ vote growth 3.7-4.4% a year; about 90% core loyalty). Derived approximation.

parameters.name: raam_dependence_penalty
parameters.value: Messages implying reliance on Ra'am lose support among about 58% of Jewish voters; only about 12.5% accept it unconditionally

open_questions: The shared web-search budget ran out mid-task (200 searches, shared across agents), so several leads could not be followed. The main ones: the Kolot Nodedim / harelc ecological vote-transfer estimates for 2019-2022, and the Levy, Rosenthal & Saporta chapter on ethnic and class voting in The Elections in Israel 2019-2021.

No verified transition matrix of 2022 vote to 2026 intention, and no crosstab of where Yashar's and Together's support comes from. Channel 12/13/Kan poll documents, or the INES March 2025 off-cycle survey listed on the INES data page, could provide one.

The direction of the October 7 effect on directly hit localities is unresolved. The rocket and terror literature predicts a rightward shift, but blame on the government (55% want a state commission of inquiry) may work against the incumbent, and Gaza-envelope kibbutzim and development towns (Sderot, Netivot, Ofakim) may respond differently.

Russian-speaking vote distribution in 2021 and 2022, and the size and leanings of the roughly 100k post-2022 immigrants from Russia and Ukraine, were not verified. The FSU turnout gap is a derived estimate.

The JPPI/Abensour page reports 39% and 22% Blue and White support among masortim attributed to INES March 2021. This looks inconsistent with Blue and White's 2021 size, and the survey wave needs checking against INES files.

Kedar (2005): I could not confirm whether Israel is among the four countries analysed (the PDF is scanned). Quantitative estimates from Bargsted & Kedar beyond the coalition-attentiveness figures were not extracted.
The J Street/Channel 12 figure (1.3% torn between blocs) comes from search-result summaries; the page returned 404 when fetched.

Locality-level masorti and secular-right shares are not published directly. They need CBS Social Survey regional estimates, the CBS religiosity-by-locality series, or proxies such as Dahan's surname method plus SES and education.

Double-envelope votes assigned to localities exist only for 2022 (obtained by petition, Atmor, Friedberg & Kenig 2025). The 2019-2021 locality turnout series lacks this correction, which complicates trend-based turnout headroom.

Whether higher Arab turnout helps or hurts the chance of preventing a Netanyahu majority depends on the Ra'am vs Joint List split and threshold risk. This needs joint simulation with the seat model, not a locality rule.
